result:
Picture a friend who is a great mechanic, on the phone, while your car is broken down. He can't see or touch the car. He only knows what you tell him. Tool calling works the same way.

The model is the mechanic on the phone. The program around it is you, standing at the car. The tools are the things you're able to do: read the dipstick, check the battery voltage, look up the booking calendar.

The key point is that the mechanic never does anything himself. He says "check the oil level and tell me what it reads." That sentence is the tool call. It's only a request. You are the one who opens the hood, reads the dipstick and reports "it's at the low mark." That report is the tool result. Then he reasons from it and either asks for another check or tells you the diagnosis.

- The model only asks. The program runs the tool.
- Each time you report back is a new call to the mechanic. He has no memory of his own, so you restate the whole conversation so far each time.
- He can only ask for checks on the list you gave him, and he picks one based on how you described it. That's why a tool's description matters.
- It ends when he gives a diagnosis instead of another request.

The analogy breaks in one place. A real mechanic remembers the earlier call. The model doesn't, so the program resends the whole history every time, and that is why long conversations cost more.

Quick check: for "Is the laser cutter free on Friday?", who actually looks at the booking calendar, the model or your program? And what happens to the calendar result next?
